issues.legal_issue: The age of a document for the ancient-document presumption is calculated from when the document is produced, not from the later date of judgment or appeal.
material_facts: The suit was filed about fifteen years after the sale deed was executed, so the deed had not reached the thirty-year period when the suit was brought.
The High Court treated the sale deed as thirty years old by counting from its execution to the date of its appellate judgment.
The lower courts gave no reason for treating the earlier lease document as proved under the ancient-document presumption.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in calculating the document’s age up to the date of its appellate decision; the presumption could not be applied to the sale deed on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Evidence Act, 1872 dispenses with the usual proof of certain old documents by raising a presumption of genuineness. The required age is reckoned backwards from the date the document is offered in evidence, not from a later judgment or appeal. The provision concerns admissibility and proof of an ancient document; its age cannot be extended by treating an appeal as a continuation of the suit.

predicates.civil_title_appeal: A party appealed a civil judgment deciding a claim to title over land.
predicates.document_was_not_thirty_years_old_when_o: The document was produced in the proceedings before it had existed for thirty years.
predicates.document_reached_thirty_years_only_by_ap: The document reached thirty years of age only by the time the appellate court decided the case.

issues.definition: When a document in a civil title appeal was not thirty years old when offered and reached that age only by the appellate decision, the ancient-document presumption does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: Possession and revenue entries do not establish title when the evidence discloses a competing title, and revenue entries are evidence of possession rather than documents of title.
material_facts: The respondent relied on its possession and revenue entries, including an entry showing another person as pattadar, to support its claim of ownership.
The respondent did not explain the pattadar’s connection to it, and that person was not joined in the suit.
Documents showed that the Government had owned the land since at least 1920.
The respondent had also paid rent to the Government and had previously sought a lease from it.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts erred in treating the revenue entries and possession as establishing title or shifting the burden to the Government; the possession-based presumption did not overcome the evidence of the Government’s title.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 110 and 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872, possession may support a rebuttable presumption of title where possession is prima facie lawful and the competing party has no title, particularly where there is no or very little proof of ownership. The presumption does not arise where the facts disclose title. A revenue record is not a document of title and raises, at most, a presumption concerning possession. The Court relied on Gurunath Manohar Pavaskar v. Nagesh Siddappa Navalgund, AIR 2008 SC 901; Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander, AIR 1968 SC 1165; and Chief Conservator of Forests, Govt. of A.P. v. Collector, AIR 2003 SC 1805. The possession principle also serves the public purpose reflected in Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Sections 154 and 158 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Acceptance of municipal or agricultural tax does not prevent the State from contesting ownership, and there can be no estoppel against a statute.

predicates.civil_land_title_claim: A party brought a civil proceeding claiming ownership of land.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_possession_or_revenue: The claimant relied on possession or revenue entries as evidence of ownership.
predicates.competing_party_has_proof_of_title: The competing party produced evidence supporting its title to the land.

issues.definition: In a civil land-title claim, when the claimant relies on possession or revenue entries and the competing party has proof of title, those matters do not establish the claimant’s title.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser does not acquire title through a sale deed when the vendor had no transferable title to the land.
material_facts: The Government had leased the land to the vendor, and the lease prohibited transfer of the land.
The vendor later executed a registered sale deed in favour of the respondent and delivered possession.
The respondent acknowledged in a letter that the vendor had no title and had misrepresented its authority to sell.
The evidence established that the vendor was only a Government lessee.
issues.conclusion: The sale deed was invalid and inoperative because the vendor was merely a lessee and had no title that could be transferred to the respondent.
issues.legal_principle: The maxim nemo dat quod non habet means that no person can give what that person does not have, and nemo plus juris tribuit quam ipse habet means that no person can confer a greater right or better title than that person possesses. A claimant relying on a sale must establish that the vendor had title capable of transfer; the purchaser cannot obtain a better title than the vendor had.

rule.if: civil_land_title_claim and claimant_derives_title_from_sale and vendor_was_only_a_lessee and vendor_had_no_transferable_title

predicates.civil_land_title_claim: A party brought a civil proceeding claiming ownership of land.
predicates.claimant_derives_title_from_sale: The claimant relied on a sale by another person as the source of the claimant’s title.
predicates.vendor_was_only_a_lessee: The person who made the sale held the land only as a lessee.
predicates.vendor_had_no_transferable_title: The person who made the sale lacked title capable of being transferred to the purchaser.

issues.definition: In a civil land-title claim, a claimant who derives title from a sale by a lessee with no transferable title acquires no title through that sale.
